title: Nine Americans rescued, 85 still missing in Nepal floods, State Department says - New York Post
description: Nine Americans rescued, 85 still missing in Nepal floods, State Department says  New York Post
publisher.title: New York Post
full_article:
Nine Americans have been safely evacuated from Nepal, but 85 are still missing after a devastating flood claimed at least 750 lives, the US State Department said Sunday.

Rescue teams are working around the clock at the Nepali-Tibetan border to search for a total of more than 3,000 missing people in the muddy ground after last week’s catastrophic flood.

“This morning, I can say we now have 85 Americans, approximately, that are unaccounted for,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott told ABC News’ “This Week.”

3 Rescue workers continue to toil at the Trishuli Center in Nepal’s Nuwakot district Sunday after catastrophic flooding hit the Nepal-Tibet border. AFP via Getty Images

3 At least 85 Americans remain missing in the disaster area, officials said. ZUMAPRESS.com

“We’ve also now seen nine Americans be safely evacuated. We are currently unaware of any US citizen deaths at this time,” he said.

The State Department has been coordinating rescue efforts with the US embassies in Tibet and China, but the remote era where the disaster took place presents logistical challenges for the search teams.

Explore More California mom makes miracle escape during Nepal flood disaster US families with relatives missing in the Nepal-China floods plead for more rescue help: ‘We don’t know anything’ Young survivor of catastrophic flooding in Nepal reunites with his mother — who feared her 2 kids were dead

“Our embassies in Beijing and Kathmandu are working 24/7 in terms of communicating and coordinating with local officials, trying to get that reliable information,” Pigott said.

The disaster took place near the Rasuwagadhi border post, where a landslide triggered horrific floods that swallowed entire villages in a single wave.

Among the missing Americans are those who traveled to Nepal to take part in a sacred Hindu and Buddhist pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, where thousands had gathered before the flood hit.

3 Rescue workers pull a person out of the mud in Nepal’s Nuwakot district last week. AFP via Getty Images

New Yorkers Amita Amin, 67, and Jitendra Manubhai Patel, 63, alongside Tejal Vyomesh Patel, 64, of New Jersey were taking part in the pilgrimage when they vanished in the disaster, Newsday reported.

The State Department has activated $3.6 million in emergency humanitarian assistance to the region, with the money set to assist 10,000 affected households, as well as the rebuilding of destroyed roads.

title: Nepal warns of more possible floods as communities grapple with devastation - AP News
description: Nepal warns of more possible floods as communities grapple with devastation  AP News
publisher.title: AP News
full_article:
DHADING, Nepal (AP) — Authorities in Nepal warned of possible fresh flooding on Sunday and urged residents in flood-affected districts to remain on high alert after water levels rose in the Bhotekoshi River.

Flood warning notices were sent to people’s phones early Sunday as rescue crews worked to clear a major highway connecting Kathmandu to one of the areas worst hit by Wednesday’s catastrophic floods , which killed at least 800 people and left more than 3,000 missing in Nepal and Tibet.

The latest warnings came after Chinese authorities informed their Nepalese counterparts of increased water flow upstream, according to Dharam Raj Uprety, chief executive of Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

The Chinese state news agency Xinhua, citing the country’s water resources ministry, said a new lake formed after Wednesday’s floods high in the mountains had largely drained.

But Xinhua said the ministry warned that a crater located 5.6 kilometers (3.5 miles) upstream, which held an estimated 1.4 million cubic meters (370 million gallons) of water, still posed some risk and required close monitoring.

Nepal’s disaster agency said Sunday the death toll had climbed to 788 with 2,502 missing, while Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing on the Chinese side of the border.

The missing include hundreds of people from over a dozen countries who were in the region to work, visit the mountains or make a pilgrimage to a sacred peak . On Sunday, Chinese state media said 261 foreigners were missing in Tibet, including over a hundred Nepalis and others from around the world.

Related Stories Saved by a lunch break: Nepal floods destroyed many schools, but students at this school survived 2 MIN READ In one Nepal district, flood catastrophe is measured in bodies and burial trenches 3 MIN READ Nepal-China flood survivors reach safe areas as families await news of nearly 3,000 missing 5 MIN READ 31

Some are returning to what remained of their homes

In Dhading, one of the worst-hit regions in Nepal, some residents began returning to ruined homes to see what can be salvaged.

Residents sat in homes with walls washed away by the floods, shoveling sludge-like mud and rubble off balconies or window frames. Others scanned the ground for items they could pick out of the mud and rinse off. One man had returned for his chickens, which he found alive. He tied them up and put them in the cabin of his truck.

“Everything is finished. Nothing is left. Not even our home,” Sharmila Tamang, a Dhading resident who was trying to salvage items from her home, told The Associated Press.

In the town of Galchhi, a group of residents sought higher ground on a nearby bridge and watched as the river roared by. Some pointed to enormous rocks washed downriver during the earlier floods, while others standing on a suspension bridge were warned off with whistles.

Along the river, homes, vehicles and farm tractors could be seen jutting from the thick gray-brown sediment that enveloped entire villages in some areas. Parts of rice terraces along the riverside had dropped into the river after landslides hit them.

Homes and businesses left intact after the flooding were still without electricity on Sunday, as twisted power line poles and wires lay tangled in the mud.

Large concrete and smaller suspension bridges were destroyed, leaving communities on the other side of the river with less easy access.

title: Death toll nears 800 in Nepal flood disaster - USA Today
description: Death toll nears 800 in Nepal flood disaster  USA Today
publisher.title: USA Today
full_article:
The death toll following a glacier collapse that unleashed a catastrophic mudslide across the Himalayas neared 800 people, authorities said on Aug. 30, as thousands of people remain missing.

Nepal's disaster authority said 781 people had died, with 2,502 missing and Chinese officials added that 16 people had died with 546 missing.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told his Nepalese counterpart during an Aug. 29 telephone call that the mudslide was their "most severe cross-border disaster" in recent years and that rescue operations had risen to an unprecedented level of difficulty and complexity, state broadcaster CCTV reported.

Dozens of Americans are included in the nearly 600 foreign nationals reported as missing by Nepal's tourism board. The board said in an Aug. 30 statement posted to social media that two Americans had been rescued and that it was "in contact" with a third. Chinese authorities said 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were unaccounted for in Tibet, near a key border crossing with Nepal.

Authorities in Nepal have begun mass burials of hundreds of unidentified victims whose bodies had started to decompose. Nearly 100 bodies were buried on Aug. 29 and 100 more are planned to be buried on Aug. 30. DNA samples were collected and burial sites carefully documented in the hope that families may still be able to identify relatives later.

"We were left with no other option," said Ganesh Aryal, chief district officer of Chitwan, told Reuters. "Our concern was the risk to public health posed by the rapid decomposition of the bodies."

Rescuers face challenging terrain

The scale of the disaster has complicated rescue efforts across the rugged Himalayan terrain as rescuers face challenging weather conditions and rising water levels.

Rescue operations have been suspended several times since Aug. 28 because of bad weather and concerns that a lake formed across the Nepal-China border by the disaster could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into Nepal's Lhende Khola and Trishuli Rivers.

Local police in Nepal told Reuters that residents and rescue workers had moved to higher ground after the Trishuli River's water levels rose on Aug. 30 following fresh rainfall, raising fears of additional flooding.

Chinese state media linked the disaster to the long-term effects of global warming. CCTV reported that the flood was a "new and prominent feature of cryosphere disasters" on the Tibetan plateau.

The Red Cross has estimated that more than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster that unfolded at about 8:30 a.m. local time on Aug. 26. A huge landslide tore through a region near the border with Tibet, sending rock, mud and debris hurtling into riverside communities. Buildings and infrastructure were destroyed and swept away.

title: Nepal flash flooding victims mourned at Everett, Massachusetts, vigil - CBS News

publisher.title: CBS News
full_article:
Dozens of people gathered at a park in Everett Saturday night to remember those killed by horrific flash flooding in Nepal.

More rain is making the rescue effort in Nepal difficult as thousands remain missing. Wednesday's disaster killed more than 670 people, destroying buildings, washing away bridges and burying towns under massive piles of debris.

A Lexington woman is among those missing.

And there are concerns about the chance for more flooding and landslides. Rescuers have pulled survivors from the mud, but it's a race against the clock now to find people still alive.

Those who came out for Saturday's vigil at Rivergreen Park in Everett are still clinging to hope.

"We are really sad. Like we're really hoping for the people that are missing. We're hoping for them to come back home safe," one woman said.

The Greater Boston Nepali community came together for a candlelit vigil not only to honor the lives lost in Nepal, but also to pray for those still missing.

"We're just trying to be all together for our country. It's a big thing going on. It's really devastating. The country is falling apart. We are just trying to get all together to be here and saying we all are with you," Ramesh Pudasaini of Everett said.

It's a tight-knit community, heartbroken by the images of catastrophic floods in their home country. For many at the vigil, relatives, friends and co-workers are still among those still missing.

"There are a couple people that I grew up with. They're still missing. We haven't heard back from them yet. The government is still doing the rescue operations. So I'm really hoping they come back safely," Sushma Adhikari said.

The Nepali community in Massachusetts is also beginning to fundraise, asking for those in attendance to contribute to relief efforts.

"Please donate as much as you can. Doesn't have to be more, doesn't have to be less. Whatever you give is helpful to us," a man at the vigil said.

All funds raised in Everett Saturday night will go to those who've lost everything amid this tragedy as homes and communities were completely destroyed. Organizers say it will be difficult to rebuild and every little bit counts.

full_article:
A student searches for her school bag from a pile extracted from the mud brought in by the recent flash floods, at the Shree Bagheswori Madhyamik School in Galchhi, Dhading district of Nepal Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. (AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha)

DHADING, Nepal — In one of the areas worst hit by Wednesday’s catastrophic floods in Nepal, a group of schoolchildren managed to survive when they happened to leave their classroom for their lunch break.

Children attending other classes at the school in Dhading also escaped because teachers told them to quickly evacuate their classrooms shortly before the waters came crashing in.

“The teachers said, ‘There is a flood and you should leave bags and tiffins,’” said Lakshmi Shrestha, the mother of a student attending the school. “That’s how they managed to survive.”

Shrestha was among mothers and children who began to return to their school on Sunday to find the kids’ belongings and see what could be salvaged. The majority of the children at the school appeared to have survived the floods, the families said.

Mud covers the floor of a classroom damaged in the recent flash floods at the Shree Bagheswori Madhyamik School in Galchhi, Dhading district of Nepal Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. (AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha)

Thick brown and gray mud coated the surfaces of school benches, walls and notebooks while the school’s courtyard was filled with sediment. Lines on the walls showed how high the water rapidly rose. A pile of small mud-caked backpacks, some with colorful key chains, were on the benches and floors, waiting to be claimed.

Kopila Mizar, the mother of a student, was unable to find her son’s backpack, but remained positive.

“My son is alive, that is my biggest happiness,” she said.

Students' lunchboxes are covered in mud brought in by the recent flash floods, at the Shree Bagheswori Madhyamik School in Galchhi, Dhading district of Nepal Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. (AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha)

At least 69 schools in Nepal’s flood-devastated districts have been destroyed or damaged, putting education at risk for nearly 19,000 children, according to the nonprofit Save the Children. Those numbers are likely to rise as rescue teams reach more areas, they said.

The government ordered schools and universities to shut down for three days following torrential rains that triggered severe flash floods and landslides across parts of the country. University exams were also paused.

With communities still receiving constant flood warnings advising them to move to higher, safer areas, it’s unclear when classes will be able to resume.

The missing include hundreds of people from over a dozen countries who were in the region to work, visit the mountains or make a pilgrimage to a sacred peak. On Sunday, Chinese state media said 261 foreigners were missing in Tibet, including over a hundred Nepalis and others from around the world.

title: ‘The river has taken everything’: people return to remains of their homes in Nepal - The Guardian
description: ‘The river has taken everything’: people return to remains of their homes in Nepal  The Guardian
publisher.title: The Guardian
full_article:
The bodies continue to wash up. But the morgues have already run out of room.

Since the deadly floods coursed through the Himalayan valleys of Nepal and Tibet, the numbers of people killed have continued to rise. The bodies have surfaced in their hundreds and continue to be pulled from the thick, tar-like mud that engulfed everything after the flood waters receded. By Sunday, the death toll stood at 804 in Nepal and Tibet.

Morgues across Nepal are already overflowing. Authorities say they are overwhelmed with the task of trying to identify the dead, many mangled beyond recognition and turning up miles from home. As places to safely store the victims run out, mass burials have begun in the district of Bharatpur.

Satellite image of Nepal showing location of Devighat

DNA samples were taken from each body before it was given a tag and a location number, wrapped in a plastic bag and then placed in a shallow grave. The hope, said the police, was that these bodies would eventually be identified by loved ones through DNA and retrieved for proper funeral rites.

In Chitwan, about 100 miles downstream from the region worst hit by the flash floods and mudslides, more than 250 bodies have washed up along the riverbanks. But they are in such a disfigured state that only nine have been successfully identified. Many will now be buried, at least temporarily, in the forest on the edge of the city.

Residents try to salvage belongings from their damaged homes

In an effort to speed up the identification exercise, local officials have adopted a macabre approach of simply asking people to go through pictures of the bodies and look for identifying features: a necklace, a wedding ring, a tattoo, a scar. Photos of those recovered have been placed on to PowerPoint slideshows, for relatives to sit patiently through, and have been uploaded to the Nepal police website. Outside the morgue in the capital, Kathmandu, photographs of the dead inside have been posted on the walls.

Yet with more than 3,000 still reported missing in Nepal and Tibet, there are fears that the numbers of dead may still rise exponentially. Many of the worst-hit areas, where entire villages were wiped away by the tidal wave of mud, water and debris, are still inaccessible except by army helicopter. Speaking on Sunday, the foreign secretary, Amrit Bahadur Rai, said the Nepal government had requested “more than 1,000 freezer units” for safe storage of the dead.

View image in fullscreen People searching for their belongings in their mud-damaged home in Devighat. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

Even in areas lower down the river valley that were decimated by the floods but have remained accessible by road, search and rescue teams have struggled to retrieve all those killed and buried in the mud. On Sunday afternoon in Devighat, a sacred town on the Trishuli River that was left in ruins by the floods, police search and rescue teams prepared to pull another victim from the muddy ruins of a house. All that was visible through the thick mud was their feet.

“It is very tough work. We have retrieved 10 bodies from here so far, maybe there will be more,” said Amabadutta Bhatta, a police superintendent working as part of search and rescue in the city. “The floods destroyed the first and second storey of most homes here. When we finally clear all the mud, which may be many months, who knows what we might find.”

Nepal-Tibet deaths from flash flooding rise amid race to free workers in tunnel Read more

Those who survived the floods in Devighat have slowly come back to see the remains of their houses, many of which were wiped away altogether. Standing next to the carcass of her house, reduced to a few concrete blocks and twisted metal, Usha Nepali, 49, wept for the home where she had raised her four children and then her three grandchildren.

View image in fullscreen People in Devighat salvage what possessions they can from their damaged homes. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

“I invested everything to build this house, so now I don’t know where to go and what to do,” said Nepali. “Nothing is left except this cloth on my back. I haven’t even been able to change clothes since the floods. How can we rebuild this house? This land is no longer safe but it’s the only land we have. The river has taken everything.”

The precariousness of living next to the Trishuli River was underlined on Sunday as the fast-moving waters again swelled dangerously high and rescuers urged people to get to higher ground quickly. Many in Devighat were packing up the few items they could find in their homes, never to return.

Jamuna Magar, 36, said her husband’s family had been living in Devighat for generations. She had come here when she got married and described it as “such a beautiful place”.

View image in fullscreen Many returned to Devighat to pack up their belongings before leaving, never to return. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

In the minutes after they got warning of the flood, she had time to grab her gold but nothing else. As she stood by the ruins of her house, clutching the only thing she had been able to retrieve so far – a plastic vat of vegetable cooking oil – she said she did not see how they could ever live in Devighat again.

“We had experienced flooding before, but we never knew a flood like this could come and take our house,” she said. “Everything we owned was on the ground floor of the house and now it’s all lost. Even our refrigerator washed away. I’m too worried about my life, about my children’s lives to stay here any longer.”

She feared it would take “decades before they can rebuild Devighat again”.

title: Live updates: Rescuers search for missing workers as death toll rises from devastating China-Nepal floods - CNN
description: Live updates: Rescuers search for missing workers as death toll rises from devastating China-Nepal floods  CNNNepal-China flood disaster: What’s the latest toll, how many are missing?  Al JazeeraNepal Turns to Mass Burials, as Thousands Remain Missing from Floods  The New York Times
publisher.title: CNN
full_article:
Mud covers a classroom at the Shree Bagheswori Madhyamik School, damaged in flash flooding in Galchhi, Dhading district, Nepal, on Sunday, Aug. 30. Niranjan Shrestha/AP

As search and rescue teams scour flood-devastated areas for the thousands of people still missing in Nepal and China, photos, videos and stories are emerging of unlikely survivors and the precarious, high-stakes operations undertaken to save them.

The flooding death toll has risen to at least 788 in Nepal, police said today, while Chinese authorities have reported at least 16 deaths.

Rescue workers from the region and international teams are racing against the clock to recover more survivors in the face of difficult post-flood conditions and lingering risks.

Here’s a recap of our latest updates:

• 6-year-old girl reunited with parents: A young girl who paramedics rescued on Friday in northern Nepal is now with her mother and father, her aunt told police. Manisha Magar was airlifted to Kathmandu following treatment, having been trapped under the rubble of collapsed buildings for 60 hours before being found.

• Students narrowly escape: In one of the worst-hit areas, a group of schoolchildren in Nepal managed to survive after they happened to leave their classroom for lunch break just in time, the Associated Press reports. Children attending other classes at the school in Dhading also escaped because teachers told them to evacuate shortly before the waters came crashing in.

• Hydropower workers: Some 279 workers from various projects, including several who spoke to CNN, have been rescued or managed to trudge their way out of the mud and silt-riddled tunnels on their own. But more than 900 workers are among those still missing, and the ongoing rescue operations at hydropower sites are some of the country’s most challenging.

• Dozens of Americans missing: At least 85 Americans are among the more than 3,000 people missing across China and Nepal, according to the US State Department. Nine Americans have been safely evacuated, a department spokesperson said Sunday morning.

• Important rescue access restored: A vital roadway to Rasuwa, one of the areas hardest hit by the flooding in Nepal, has been opened today, giving aid groups desperately needed ground access, said David Fisher, who heads the Nepal delegation for the International Federation of the Red Cross.

• Bodies buried in forest: Officials in southern Nepal were forced to lay 199 unidentified bodies to rest in the middle of a forest over recent days, according to police, after medical stocks to preserve the remains for DNA testing dwindled. The remains were among 272 bodies recovered after being swept south from Tibet toward a district in Nepal that borders India, a local police inspector told CNN on Sunday.

title: Headteacher saves 900 children from deadly flash flood in Nepal - The Guardian
description: Headteacher saves 900 children from deadly flash flood in Nepal  The Guardian
publisher.title: The Guardian
full_article:
A headteacher in Nepal evacuated 900 children from a school moments before a deadly wall of water struck their town amid the devastating flash floods that have killed almost 800 people and left thousands missing.

Rajendra Dawadi decided to halt classes and order children to higher ground after receiving warnings about the scale of the flooding heading their way.

Dawadi, the headteacher at Tribhuvan Trishuli secondary school in Nuwakot, which has 1,600 pupils, said he had received four warnings from different people within minutes, including one from Betrawati, a town directly upstream.

Rajendra Dawadi, the headteacher of Tribhuvan Trishuli secondary school in Nuwakot

This prompted him to take immediate action. “I decided I shouldn’t delay any more,” he told the BBC. “Even if the flood was not coming, it was just a matter of a single day’s classes.”

Dawadi said during the evacuation of the school he saw a hostel building about 100 metres from the river being engulfed by the torrent of flood water.

“If we had made the decision 10 minutes later, all of us, including the students and me, would not be able to speak to you today,” he said.

One student said Dawadi’s decision had saved their lives with moments to spare. Yunisha, 16, told reporters: “I, along with my friends, survived by just 10 seconds.”

She described the children running up a muddy path to escape as water and debris inundated the town. “Within no time, the bazaar was swept away in front of my eyes,” she said. She was reunited with her family three days later.

‘The river has taken everything’: people return to remains of their homes in Nepal Read more

At least 69 schools have been destroyed or damaged by the floods, affecting nearly 19,000 children, according to the charity Save the Children.

In Dhading, one of the areas worst hit by the floods, a group of schoolchildren survived the disaster when they left their classroom for their lunch break.

Others in the area escaped when teachers told them to quickly evacuate classrooms just before the waters came crashing in.

The mother of one child told the Associated Press that teachers had warned students: “There is a flood and you should leave bags and tiffins. That’s how they managed to survive.”

More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. The country said on Sunday 2,502 people, including 592 foreigners, were out of contact. It reported an updated death toll of 781 people.

The disaster, which struck the Nepal-Tibet border region of the Himalayas on Wednesday morning, was caused by a glacial collapse that sent a wall of water and debris cascading downstream, the US Geological Survey said.

Nepal’s foreign minister has called for a global response to the climate crisis, saying the Nepali people had disproportionately become “major victims of climate change” despite having contributed a fraction of the planet’s fossil fuel emissions.

Updated: 3:57 PM EDT Aug 30, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Jeff Stitt Digital Curator

Authorities in Nepal warned of possible fresh flooding on Sunday and urged residents in flood-affected districts to remain on high alert after water levels rose in the Bhotekoshi River.

Flood warning notices were sent to people's phones early Sunday as rescue crews worked to clear a major highway connecting Kathmandu to one of the areas worst hit by Wednesday's catastrophic floods, which killed at least 800 people and left more than 3,000 missing in Nepal and Tibet.

The latest warnings came after Chinese authorities informed their Nepalese counterparts of increased water flow upstream, according to Dharam Raj Uprety, chief executive of Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

The Chinese state news agency Xinhua, citing the country’s water resources ministry, said a new lake formed after Wednesday’s floods high in the mountains had largely drained.

But Xinhua said the ministry warned that a crater located 5.6 kilometers (3.5 miles) upstream, which held an estimated 1.4 million cubic meters of water, still posed some risk and required close monitoring.

Nepal’s disaster agency said Sunday the death toll had climbed to 788 with 2,502 missing, while Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing on the Chinese side of the border.

The missing include hundreds of people from over a dozen countries who were in the region to work, visit the mountains or make a pilgrimage to a sacred peak. On Sunday, Chinese state media said 261 foreigners were missing in Tibet, including over a hundred Nepalis and others from around the world.



Some are returning to what remained of their homes

In Dhading, one of the worst-hit regions in Nepal, some residents began returning to ruined homes to see what can be salvaged.

Residents sat in homes with walls washed away by the floods, shoveling sludge-like mud and rubble off balconies or window frames. Others scanned the ground for items they could pick out of the mud and rinse off. One man had returned for his chickens, which he found alive. He tied them up and put them in the cabin of his truck.

“Everything is finished. Nothing is left. Not even our home,” Sharmila Tamang, a Dhading resident who was trying to salvage items from her home, told The Associated Press.

At a key power plant that was severely damaged by the floods, workers started inspecting the facilities Sunday to survey the destruction. The plant serves over 20,000 people across four districts.

In the town of Galchhi, a group of residents sought higher ground on a nearby bridge and watched as the river roared by. Some pointed to enormous rocks washed downriver during the earlier floods, while others standing on a suspension bridge were warned off with whistles.

Along the river, homes, vehicles and farm tractors could be seen jutting from the thick gray-brown sediment that enveloped entire villages in some areas. Parts of rice terraces along the riverside had dropped into the river after landslides hit them.

Residents are receiving constant flood warnings

Homes and businesses left intact after the flooding were still without electricity on Sunday, as twisted power line poles and wires lay tangled in the mud.

Residents of flood-hit villages said they were struggling to make sense of near-constant alarms they've received since the initial floods.

“Sometimes they say a flood is coming, then we have to run again to higher ground, even at night. There is also rain,” said Govind Shreshta, a resident. “It’s really difficult for me. I have a 72-year-old father and 70-year-old mom. I must carry them and I am exhausted. It’s going on like this for those who are still alive.”

Large concrete and smaller suspension bridges were destroyed, leaving communities on the other side of the river with less easy access.

“Those who are there are now stuck there. Those who are here are stuck here. It’s going to be very difficult,” said Sattan Singh Tamang, 47, who was working near a bridge when Wednesday’s floods came.

Minister says Nepalis have become victims of climate change

Wednesday’s flash floods started after a glacial collapse high in the Himalayan region. Scientists who studied satellite images said bedrock underneath a glacier high in the Himalayan region had collapsed, taking part of the glacier with it. The rockfall was so extreme that it registered as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake.

The rocks and melted water then swelled the rivers in the valleys below, causing a torrent of water that swept buildings, bridges and earth downstream in Tibet and Nepal.

Related video below: Comparative satellite image of Nepal-China border

Nepal’s foreign minister called for a global response to climate change, saying Nepal was bearing a disproportionate share of its impact.

“Despite having only 0.1% contribution to the global emissions, people of Nepal have become major victims of climate change,” Shisir Khanal said Saturday.

Scientists have said it is too early to draw a direct connection between global warming and Wednesday’s catastrophe. However, they said that as Earth’s temperature rises because of human activities such as burning oil, gas and coal, the chances of such disasters increase, especially in the Himalayan mountains, which are warming considerably faster than many other parts of the world.

Meanwhile, Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Sunday his country will send a search-and-rescue team to Nepal to assist with relief efforts and help evacuate Malaysians affected by the disaster.

Malaysia has also pledged $1 million in financial aid to Nepal, he said in a statement.

full_article:
Fifteen British nationals are reported to be missing in China as the search continues for survivors of the devastating flooding in Nepal and Tibet.

Nepali and Chinese authorities confirmed an updated death toll of at least 810 on Sunday. More than 3,000 people are believed missing after flash floods triggered by a massive glacier collapse in the Himalayas on Wednesday engulfed Gyirong port on the Nepal-China border.

‘The river has taken everything’: people return to remains of their homes in Nepal Read more

The 15 missing British people are among 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries missing in China, according to figures released by Chinese authorities, bringing the total of missing Britons between Tibet and Nepal to 48. The Tibet autonomous region’s government said the total missing there also included 104 Nepalis, 49 people from India, 33 from Latvia and 18 from the US.

Thirty-three British people had already been declared missing on the Nepal side of the border. Some were on a pilgrimage at the time of the flood, including Hemangini Jitendra Patel and Hema Sunil Amin, two sisters who were last seen on the Friendship Bridge on the border.

The figure for missing Americans has been disputed by the US state department, which declared on Sunday that at least 85 US citizens were missing. The department’s spokesperson, Tommy Pigott, said getting accurate information from the region had been difficult, “made even more so by the devastation and the remoteness that we see”.

Chinese authorities have said at least 16 people have died on their side of the border. But there are concerns over a possible lack of transparency from the Chinese government, which has prevented footage of the floods from being shared in the country and may have downplayed the casualties.

Police in Nepal said 794 people had been confirmed to have died there and at least 2,742 injured. Numerous areas remain at risk of fresh flooding and people who have returned to their homes have been told to remain alert and be prepared to evacuate again at short notice.

View image in fullscreen Army personnel conduct a search and rescue operation for flood victims along the Narayani River in Nepal’s Chitwan district on Sunday. Photograph: Prakash Mathema/AFP/Getty Images

Rescue efforts have been affected by the threat of landslides and dangerous weather as well as confusion over which side of the border victims had been on when the waters struck.

Chinese state television reported that officials in Beijing, far better resourced than their Nepali counterparts, had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated more than 220m yuan (£24m) to support relief efforts.

Equipment and supplies have been airdropped to frontline workers, while Chinese soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing, CCTV said. The Chinese premier, Li Qiang, had already travelled to the region.

Numerous countries have pledged to help Nepal, including the US, which has offered $3.6m (£2.7m) in humanitarian aid, “including up to three months of emergency food assistance to up to 10,000 flood-affected households”, on top of $500,000 previously pledged, and Australia, which will donate more than $3m in assistance.

Britain has committed £5m to Nepal and sent a rapid deployment team, which arrived in Kathmandu on Saturday.

A UK Foreign Office spokesperson said: “We are working around the clock to support British nationals and their families affected by the devastating floods on the Nepal-China border. We are coordinating closely with the Nepali and Chinese authorities and have deployed consular support staff to the region to ensure British nationals can access support.”

Rai's husband, Sanjeev Rai, has now traveled to Nepal to try to find his wife, overwhelmed by the horrific and unbearable search to find his wife. He is now among the thousands searching morgues and hospitals for lost loved ones.

"He's overwhelmed. He's been breaking down -- many times. You call him and you can hear him crying," Singh Meet said.

At least 90 Americans were missing as of Friday, according to the State Department. Local officials in Nepal report that nearly 700 bodies have been found, and more than 3,000 people are still missing.

On Saturday, Singh Meet flew out of Logan Airport to help Rai's husband try to search for her. He too is desperate to find his friend of over 15 years, a woman who has been alongside him in their journey from India to the United States.

Rai is a "joyful" and devoted mother to two children, a 22-year-old daughter, and a 15-year-old son, Singh Meet said, and has spent years as an engineer with Intel in Hudson.

"Everyone is devastated. We need closure," he said.

Singh Meet's and Rai's families are deeply intertwined, only living a mile apart in Lexington.

"That's the least I could do, right? That's the least I could do," Singh Meet said. "There are relationships beyond love, beyond friendship. Sometimes, you are so well connected with each other, with your families and everything. There are no ifs and buts. You don't think twice. You just go, and you know you're there for each other."

Singh Meet is determined to get closure for Rai's family, he said, as he prays for every soul lost, and every person left behind.

"If she is alive, keep her alive and give us the strength to bring her back. Give her the strength to be fine and come back. If she has really left for our heavenly abode, then please help us find her, and please help everyone else find their loved ones because everyone has to have this closure with them," Singh Meet said.
